newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basque Guggenheim denied fragile Picasso Guernica.
newsitem.headline: Basque Guggenheim denied fragile Picasso Guernica.

text.p: Spain's Reina Sofia contemporary art museum refused on Tuesday to loan Pablo Picasso's anti-war masterpiece "Guernica" to the new Guggenheim in the Basque region saying it was too fragile to move.

The Guggenheim Museum, opening on October 3 in the Basque city of Bilbao, had hoped to use Picasso's emblematic depiction of the 1937 blanket bombing by German planes of Basque nationalist shrine Guernica as its inaugural centrepiece.

But Reina Sofia officials told a new conference on Tuesday that conservation of the 60-year-old work of art, one of the most famous this century, was more important than any symbolic gesture toward the Basque museum.

"The Guernica is enormously valuable in the history of contemporary art and its physical state must be looked after," Valeriano Bozal, president of the museum's patrons, said. "It should not be moved to another museum."
Reina Sofia conservationist Pilar Sedano said the vast canvas, measuring almost 12 feet by 26 (3.6 by 7.8 metres), had suffered too much in previous moves to risk another transfer.

"It has already been moved 32 times and because of its size it's very difficult to move without causing more damage," Sedano told Reuters. "For this reason I think it's better to try to keep it here and at least conserve it in the state it's in."

The "Guernica", painted on commission from the Republican government for the World's Fair in Paris during Spain's 1936-39 Civil War, portrays agonised figures and animals in stark black, grey and white tones.

The painting, which still provokes strong reactions among Spaniards, was shown around the world as a symbol of the horrors of war but, at Picasso's request, was only brought to Spain in 1981 after democracy was restored.
